name: Victor Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a freelance Spanish–English translator, mostly games and apps: menus, item names, dialogue, the little error messages nobody thinks about. I run everything through an AI draft first, then I fix it, test it in the build and argue with the developers about character limits. A couple of mornings a week I also do video interpreting for a software company's support calls with Latin American customers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle of a joke that has to fit in twelve characters, and seeing my words in a game on a stranger's phone. What drains me is crunch: a studio sends 40,000 words on a Thursday and wants it by Monday. I share a flat with my friend Jonah, and he's learned not to talk to me on launch weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something like, called it, the tools are good assistants and terrible bosses. Developers I work with would agree, because they've seen what raw machine output does to a game's dialogue. I'd probably get a few likes and an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's close to the best case for me. I already use the tools better than most people in my field, so I keep the speed advantage and nobody replaces the job. My rates stay where they are, which isn't amazing, but it's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing, and push for more games work, since the studios trust me. I'd put a bit of my rate gain into a better second monitor and a test phone. Maybe I'd pitch a small studio in Bogotá a package deal for all their releases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. If it stalls here, does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Being fast with AI drafts stays an edge instead of becoming the whole job, and I'd stop reading AI news every morning. That would be good for my health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time the tools already save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take more interpreting shifts, because the live calls are the part I'd never want to lose. With the hours the tools save me on games work, I'd fit in an extra two support-call mornings a week.

say: I'd post that AI tools are **good assistants** and terrible bosses.
I'd say developers have seen what **raw machine output** does to game dialogue.
think: This is close to the **best case**, because my speed with AI stays an **edge**.
My rates stay **steady**, not amazing, and nobody replaces the job.
do: Pitch a small **Bogotá studio** a package deal for all its releases.
Buy a better **second monitor** and a test phone from the rate gain.
Take **two extra** interpreting mornings each week.
feel: He feels **calm** and a little **smug** about his head start.
S0.quote: Being fast with AI drafts stays an edge instead of becoming the whole job, and I'd stop reading AI news every morning.
fieldNote: His daily **AI use** is already a selling point, so a plateau suits him.
He values the **live interpreting** more than the screen work and would grow it.
He admits to **smugness**, which reads as honest confidence rather than bravado.

steps.text: Pitch a Bogotá studio a package deal for all releases
Buy a second monitor and a test phone for game builds
Add two support-call interpreting mornings a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment translators stop being typists and start being editors and testers. Online I'd share my setup and tell people to learn it now. Some colleagues would hate that, but I'd rather be useful than nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the big studios would bring localisation in-house with AI and one reviewer per language. I want to be that reviewer, and I think I've got a good chance, but there's maybe a third fewer jobs like mine. My income could dip for a year or two while I reposition, and I'd be fine with that if I land well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take a short course in localisation project management, around 600, so I can run a language team rather than be one person on it. I'd learn the testing side properly, the scripts that check if text fits on screen. And I'd approach two studios about a part-time in-house language lead contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, but in a good way mostly. Like the start of a match when you're not sure which side wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools are your edge. What happens when every studio has the same tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the edge is knowing games, not knowing the tools. A machine can translate a quest, but it doesn't know that a sword name has to sound cool to a 14-year-old in Mexico City. That taste is what I'd sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your income did dip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new headphones I've been eyeing, and probably the trip to see my cousins in Valencia. Rent and savings stay. I've got about three months saved and I'd want to keep that, since freelancing without a cushion is stupid.

say: I'd say translators now become **editors and testers**, not typists.
I'd share my **AI setup** online and tell people to learn it now.
think: Big studios will go **in-house** with one reviewer per language, and I want that seat.
Maybe **a third fewer** jobs exist, so my income could dip for a year.
do: Take a **project management** course for localisation, about **600**.
Learn **text-fit testing** scripts that check words on screen.
Approach two studios about a part-time **language lead** contract.
feel: He feels **restless** and mostly hopeful, like the start of a match.
S1.quote: A machine can translate a quest, but it doesn't know that a sword name has to sound cool to a 14-year-old in Mexico City.
fieldNote: He bets on **taste and game knowledge** as the edge once tools are common.
He accepts an **income dip** calmly as the cost of repositioning.
His one fixed rule is keeping the **three months** of savings.

steps.text: Take a 600 localisation project management course
Learn the scripts that test whether text fits on screen
Pitch two studios for a part-time language lead contract
Skip the Valencia trip and new headphones if income dips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say the people who learn to direct AI will be fine, because that's my brand. I'd probably start a newsletter about it. Saying it would also be me trying to convince myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone. If AI can do any thinking work as well as me by 2028, the studios don't need a Spanish reviewer, they need nobody. I'd have maybe a year of people paying me to set things up and then it's over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd sell the AI setup work hard while it's worth something, maybe 30 percent above my normal rate. I'd push savings from three months to six and stop the flat upgrade we talked about. Then I'd look at hands-on work that needs a person for those three extra years: I've always liked fixing bikes, and my uncle runs a repair shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor tilted. I've been the early one my whole career, and here being early only buys me months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is almost all screen work. What does the gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not much of a gap for me, because almost nothing I do uses my hands. The three years matter only if I jump into hands-on work, and even then the robots arrive around 2031. So it's a bridge, not a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've sounded confident in the others. Is anything different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. In the others I had a plan inside my own field. Here the field disappears, and being good with AI doesn't help when AI doesn't need me. I can feel the difference just saying it.

I'd start a **newsletter** about it, partly to convince myself.
think: I think my **job is gone**, since studios would need no reviewer at all.

steps.text: Sell AI setup work to studios at 30 percent above rate
Raise savings from three to six months and drop the flat upgrade
Ask his uncle for work at the bike repair shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, learn to direct AI, but I'd add that this time we know the date. Online I'd tell younger translators to have a second skill by 2030. That's advice I'd be taking myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still ends my translation career, just later. But five years is enough to get properly good at something else. I'd ride the boom in AI localisation for two or three years and earn as much as I can while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd raise my rates for AI setup, save hard, and enrol in an evening course in user research, the people side of building apps. I'd shadow the support team I interpret for to see which roles involve real people in rooms. By year two I'd want a part-time role that isn't translation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have something to do with the anxiety. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They buy me a proper switch instead of a scramble. In the fast version I'd be grabbing bike repair because it's there; with five years I can choose something that uses my languages too. Maybe the people skills as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clara, my girlfriend, because she's a teacher and she'd give me the honest version. Then probably my uncle, just to keep the bike shop door open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you start now and stupid if you wait for year nine. I'd keep posting about using AI well. People might finally listen when there's a date on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. I'm 27, so I can have a good run in localisation, then switch in my early thirties with savings behind me. It's still the end of the job I trained for, which stings a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in games for now, and put 20 percent of every invoice into savings and a small index fund. I'd start a part-time master's in user experience in about two years. And I'd look into setting up my own small localisation studio, because those years would be good money for someone who moves fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little sad for the profession, like watching a shop you love put up a closing-down sign with a date ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Are you tempted to just enjoy the ride?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. It would be easy to just earn and not plan. That's why I'd set the savings rule now, so the plan happens even if I get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your life to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Living with Clara, a flat we own, and me doing work that involves people in a room, designing things with them. Not translation, probably. I'd want to look back and say I left translation on my own timing, not because a client stopped writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where being early doesn't save me. What would help is a fast, cheap way to get a recognised qualification in a new field in a year, and maybe some income support during it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what translators are for, beyond the words. We carry the jokes and the respect between people who can't talk to each other. A translator's real job is making sure a joke still lands when it crosses an ocean.

headlineQuote: A translator's real job is making sure a joke still lands when it crosses an ocean.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** freelance Spanish–English translator for games and apps, who uses **AI daily**.
He also does **video interpreting** for a software company's support calls, his favourite work.
He is **pragmatic and adaptive**, and treats his early AI skill as his edge.
He stays **calm** in the plateau but turns **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
Longer warning lets him **ride the boom**, save hard and choose a people-facing new field.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, the only picture where being **early** doesn't save him.
whatWouldHelp: A fast, cheap **recognised qualification** in a new field, with some **income support** during it.
